item.title: Week1 - Introduction
item.description:
This week, I give an introduction to the course and some study tips. Then we discuss the words statement, formula and proof and learn about the basics of propositional logic.

Resources

See Week2.

Useful Links

  • THE SCRIPT is your main rescource for the course
  • D-INFK discord
  • moodle course page
  • diskmath.ch is a website maintained by multiple TAs. It contains explanations, tutorials, exercises and more for a lot of the topics from the lecture
  • old course page contains a timeline of the lectures last year
  • eduapp shows your timetable and contains a campus map
  • eth videoportal lets you watch the recorded lectures afterwards
  • VIS website contains the exam collection
  • shivi.io maintained by another TA, contains lecture notes for the first year subjects
  • algebra book “Abstract Algebra: Theory and Applications” is a nice, freely available book if you want to get another perspective on / dive deeper into algebra

Exercise Sheet Recommendations

All exercises this week are important and you should have a look at them. Don’t forget to hand in 1.5 to receive bonus points! For 1.6 remember to only apply one rule each step and exactly that rule. Even if some steps might be obvious to you, being exact is very important in Diskmath and you should start developing good habits early on.

item.title: Week2 - Predicate Logic
item.description:
This week we recap propositional logic and discuss the formalism needed in the exercises. Then I introduce predicate logic and we practice working with quantifiers and predicates.

Resources

  • Slides: pdf
  • Kahoot: link
  • Exercises: pdf

Notes on Last Exercise Sheet

  • You only need to hand in the bonus. If you need feedback for another exercise please tell me directly, per default I will only correct the bonus.
  • Read the task description carefully and make sure you satisfy everything it asks from you. If the tasks says “argue by comparing truth tables” you need to compute a truth table and argue with a sentence.
  • Every proof should end with a sentence like “This is what I showed and therefore I conclude the statement is true”. Make it clear what exactly you proved and why you think you proved it.
  • Use correct notation. Don’t make up your own abbreviations. (If you do so, you need to explain them.)
  • When you do truth tables, start with 000 at the top and end with 111 at the bottom (convention).
  • In general, your submissions this week looked very good and I could see that most of you understood the topic well [:

Predicate Logic

Last week we worked a lot with propositional logic and symbols like ¬,∨,∧,→,A,B\lnot , \lor , \land , \rightarrow , A , B¬,∨,∧,→,A,B. But those types of formulas are very limited in their expression. Predicate Logic adds new symbols which allow us to express more concepts in our formulas:

Predicates are functions Uk→{0,1}U^k \rightarrow \{0,1\}Uk→{0,1}. They take k values from the universe UUU and then give a truth value depending on them. Whenever we want to work with predicates we need to specify the universe we are working in.

An easy way to define a predicate is specifying when exactly it yields true. For example

P(x)=1⟺x is prime P(x)=1 \Longleftrightarrow x \thinspace \text{is prime} P(x)=1⟺xis prime

defines a precidate P that gives true exactly when its input is prime.

Warning

The universe is very important! Interpreting the formula ∀x∃y(y<x)\forall x \exists y (y < x)∀x∃y(y<x) with U=NU=\mathbb{N}U=N or U=ZU=\mathbb{Z}U=Z makes a big difference.

Quantifiers allow us to reason about the elements in the universe:

  • ∀xP(x)\forall x P(x)∀xP(x) means “P(x)P(x)P(x) is true for all xxx in UUU”
  • ∃xP(x)\exists x P(x)∃xP(x) means “there exists some (at least one) xxx in UUU for which P(x)P(x)P(x) is true.

Warning

∃x\exists x∃x does not mean “exactly one”

Negating Quantifiers

When we negate a quantifier, we pull the ¬\lnot¬ inside and change the quantifier. So

¬∀xP(x)≡∃x¬P(x) \lnot \forall x P(x) \equiv \exists x \lnot P(x) ¬∀xP(x)≡∃x¬P(x)

and

¬∃xP(x)≡∀x¬P(x) \lnot \exists x P(x) \equiv \forall x \lnot P(x) ¬∃xP(x)≡∀x¬P(x)

Make sure to read the chapters in the script about predicate logic. If you need some more practice, look at the page on discmath.ch

Exercise Sheet Recommendations

All exercises this week are important! 2.4 is a very fun riddle, but don’t worry if you cannot solve it. For 2.3, make sure that you only apply one rule per step and apply them exactly as in Lemma 2.1. Specifically:

  • Double negation (¬¬A≡A\lnot \lnot A \equiv A¬¬A≡A) is a rule.
  • Associativity is a rule. You cannot just reorder brackets.
  • The rules in Lemma 2.1 all have a direction. If the rule says A∨(A∧B)≡AA \lor (A \land B) \equiv AA∨(A∧B)≡A then it says exactly that, and not (A∧B)∨A≡A(A \land B) \lor A \equiv A(A∧B)∨A≡A.

Also read carefully exactly what requirements your final formula needs to fulfill. The task is very doable, so be sure to be exact so you get your well-deserved bonus points.

item.title: Week3 - Proof Patterns
item.description:
This week we focus a lot on proof patterns since it is a very important topic. We also quickly review predicate logic.

Resources

  • Slides: pdf
  • Proof Examples: pdf
  • Kahoot: link made by Tobias Steinbrecher <3
  • Statements vs Formulas: pdf (in German)

Notes on Last Exercise Sheet

  • Overall the submissions were very good (:
  • Be careful when you apply rules to larger formulas. You still need to keep the brackets. For example ¬(A∧B)∨C\lnot (A \land B) \lor C¬(A∧B)∨C becomes (¬A∨¬B)∨C(\lnot A \lor \lnot B) \lor C(¬A∨¬B)∨C when using de Morgans rule!
  • By now you probably figured out that the grading scheme can be very strict, so don’t be too discouraged if you lost a lot of points.

Proving Proof Patterns with Propositional Logic

Okay, we we already know a lot of proof patterns. But what if we want to create our own one and show that it is actually correct? Or what if someone gives us a proof pattern they came up with and we want to show them that it does not work?

We can do both of those things using propositional logic! I will explain the idea first and then give examples for both proving and disproving a proof pattern.

When you are asked to evaluate a proof pattern, it will always be of the following form: It states what statement SSS it wants to prove and then gives some other statements. Then it claims if we prove those other statements, we have actually proven the statement SSS. For example, a proposed proof pattern might look like this:

We want to prove the statement SSS, we first prove another statement TTT. Then we show that T  ⟹  ST \implies ST⟹S

This proof pattern consists of two parts (which should prove SSS):

  1. We prove TTT
  2. We prove T  ⟹  ST \implies ST⟹S

You might also see proof patterns with more steps and parts. Don’t get confused! The first step is always to find out what statements the pattern consists of.

Great, but how do we work with the proof pattern now? Here is where the logic part comes in. We can actually rewrite the pattern using propositional logic. To do this, we take each of the statements, convert them to propositional logic and then combine them with ∧\land∧. To avoid confusion, we use the letters A,B,C,…A, B, C, \dotsA,B,C,… in our formulas and let their truth values correspond to the truth of the statements. For our example proof pattern this would look like this:

We choose the symbol AAA and BBB, which correspond to the statements SSS and TTT and their truth values respectively. Now we rewrite the statements in propositional logic:

  1. “We prove TTT” becomes BBB
  2. “We prove T  ⟹  ST \implies ST⟹S” becomes B→AB \rightarrow AB→A

Combining those we get: F=B∧(B→A)F = B \land (B \rightarrow A)F=B∧(B→A)

Okay, we tranformed our statements to a formula FFF. But how do we reason about the correctness of the proof pattern? There is actually a very simple rule:

The proof pattern is correct exactly if:

F⊨A F \vDash A F⊨A

Where FFF is the formula we get from the proof pattern and AAA is the logical variable corresponding to the statement we want to prove. This means we can disprove a proof pattern by showing:

F⊭A F \nvDash A F⊭A

Why does this work? We want to show that our statement SSS is true if we proved all the other statements. Our formula FFF evaluating to true represents the fact that all the statements are true (since we “linked” each propositional variable to a statement and combined them with ∧\land∧). If F⊨AF \vDash AF⊨A then this means that if all our statements are actually true (FFF is true), then SSS must also be true (AAA is true). If the logic consequence does not hold, then there must exist some truth assignment where FFF gives true but AAA is set to false. This means that SSS can be false even if all our statements are true, which means the pattern is not valid.

If the statement you want to show is not simply one statement SSS, but for example S  ⟹  TS \implies TS⟹T, then you need to transform that to propositional logic too and show the consequence. This should look like:

F⊨(A→B) F \vDash (A \rightarrow B) F⊨(A→B)

So let’s finish our small example. We show that F⊨AF \vDash AF⊨A:

F=B∧(B→A)≡B∧(¬B∨A)≡(B∧¬B)∨(B∧A)≡⊥∨(B∧A)≡B∧A⊨A \begin{align*} F & = B \land (B \rightarrow A) \\\\ & \equiv B \land (\lnot B \lor A) \\\\ & \equiv (B \land \lnot B) \lor (B \land A) \\\\ & \equiv \bot \lor (B \land A) \\\\ & \equiv B \land A \\\\ & \vDash A \end{align*} F​=B∧(B→A)≡B∧(¬B∨A)≡(B∧¬B)∨(B∧A)≡⊥∨(B∧A)≡B∧A⊨A​

Step by Step

Let’s go over the method step by step again before we do some examples:

### Extract the Statements See what statement $S$ should be proved by the pattern. Then find all the statements we use to prove that statement. (It does not need to be named $S$, we just assume that here for simplicity.)

Transform the Statements to Prop. Logic

Define propositional variables A,B,…A,B, \dotsA,B,… for the statements. Transform each statement individually and then combine them with ∧\land∧ to get a formula FFF.

(Dis)prove the Cogical Consequence

You can prove F⊨AF \vDash AF⊨A either by equivalence transformations or truth tables. You can disprove it by finding a truth assignment where FFF gives true but AAA is set to false.

Example 1: Proving Correctness

This is an exercise from 2020. We get the following proof pattern and want to show that it is correct:

To prove SSS: Find statements UUU and TTT. Prove TTT, assuming SSS is false. Prove UUU, assuming SSS is false. Show that not both TTT and UUU are true.

Step 1: We have three statements here:

  1. not S   ⟹  \implies⟹ T
  2. not S   ⟹  \implies⟹ U
  3. not both U and T are true

Those statements should show S.

Step 2: We use AAA for SSS, BBB for TTT and CCC for UUU. The formulas are:

  1. ¬A→B\lnot A \rightarrow B¬A→B
  2. ¬A→C\lnot A \rightarrow C¬A→C
  3. ¬(B∧C)\lnot (B \land C)¬(B∧C)

Combining them we get:

(¬A→B)∧(¬A→C)∧¬(B∧C) (\lnot A \rightarrow B) \land (\lnot A \rightarrow C) \land \lnot (B \land C) (¬A→B)∧(¬A→C)∧¬(B∧C)

Step 3: To show that the proof pattern is correct we now need to show:

(¬A→B)∧(¬A→C)∧¬(B∧C)⊨A (\lnot A \rightarrow B) \land (\lnot A \rightarrow C) \land \lnot (B \land C) \vDash A (¬A→B)∧(¬A→C)∧¬(B∧C)⊨A

You can use a truth table to show that this holds. This shows that the proof pattern is indeed correct.

Example 2: Disproving Correctness

We want to show that the following proof pattern is incorrect:

To prove S  ⟹  TS \implies TS⟹T we find a statement RRR and prove that R is true. Then we show that if RRR is true, SSS must be true. Finally, we show that at least one of RRR and TTT must be true.

Step 1: We want to show S  ⟹  TS \implies TS⟹T using three statements:

  1. RRR is true
  2. R  ⟹  S R\implies SR⟹S
  3. RRR or TTT (or both) must be true

Step 2: We use AAA for SSS, BBB for TTT and CCC for RRR. The formulas are:

  1. CCC
  2. C→AC \rightarrow AC→A
  3. C∨BC \lor BC∨B

Combined we get:

C∧(C→A)∧(C∨B) C \land (C \rightarrow A) \land (C \lor B) C∧(C→A)∧(C∨B)

Step 3: We want to show that:

C∧(C→A)∧(C∨B)⊭A→B C \land (C \rightarrow A) \land (C \lor B) \nvDash A \rightarrow B C∧(C→A)∧(C∨B)⊭A→B

Note that we transformed the statement the pattern tries to prove into A→BA \rightarrow BA→B.

For the truth assignment A=1,B=0,C=1A=1, B=0, C=1A=1,B=0,C=1 the left hand side evaluates to true, but the right hand side evaluates to false. This shows that the proof pattern is not valid.

Proof Patterns

Read the script and look at discmath.ch for more examples. The proof patterns are very standard so you can also find good explanations on the internet.

Exercise Sheet Recommendations

Do all the exercises! 3.6 2) is a three-star, but actually not that difficult (and very similar to the example in the script if you need a hint), so definitely try it!

item.title: Week4 - Sets
item.description:
This week we introduce sets and the basic set operations. Then we practive proving properties / equalities of sets and talk about relations a bit.

Resources

  • Feedback Form: link
  • Slides: pdf
  • Kahoot: link
  • Exercises: pdf
  • Mega Summary: pdf

Notes on Last Exercise Sheet

  • Overall the submissions were quite good, most problems were not about understanding but presentation.
  • You should always use brackets to make the precedence in your formulas clear.
  • Use the correct arrows (look at week 3 for a guide).
  • Read the task carefully! If it says “do it this way” then you have to do it this way.
  • Explain what you are doing! It is not enough if the solution makes sense in you head. A proof needs to be exact and cannot leave room for interpretation.
  • Be careful about restrictions in the exercise. You need to be precise in Diskmath! If “<” is a predicate does not mean that “>” is also one.
  • You proof should begin with “We prove … by showing …” and end with “This proves the statement by …”. If you cannot describe (or at least have a general idea about) 1) what you want to prove 2) what you need to do to prove it 3) how you are going to do that, then you should not start writing the proof yet.

About Sets

Sets are some of the most important objects in mathematics. A lot of things (like the natural numbers) are derived from set theory. If you want to read more on how we define sets, you can look at discmath.ch or search for “ZFK Axioms” online.

So what is a set? For us, the hintrmal definition “a collection of well defined objects” should be enough. We write a∈Aa \in Aa∈A if aaa is an element of AAA.

Caution

A set can only contain each element once. This means an object is either inside the set or not.

The script contains a very good explanation for the set operations like ⊆\subseteq⊆, ∪\cup∪, … Make sure that you not only understand them intuitively, but also the formal definitions.

The Powerset

One of the more difficult set operations is the powerset of a set.

We define the powerset of a set AAA as:

S∈P(A)⟺S⊆A S \in P(A) \Longleftrightarrow S \subseteq A S∈P(A)⟺S⊆A

w In words: “the powerset of A contains all subsets of A”.

Note that the powerset is a set which contains sets. It has the following interesting properties:

  • A∈P(A)A \in P(A)A∈P(A)
  • ∅∈P(A)\varnothing \in P(A)∅∈P(A) for any set AAA
  • AAA is not necessarily a subset of P(A)P(A)P(A)! P(A)P(A)P(A) contains sets, which contain elements of AAA. But it does not (necessarily) contain the elements of AAA.
  • ∣A∣=k  ⟹  ∣P(A)∣=2k|A| = k \implies |P(A)| = 2^{k}∣A∣=k⟹∣P(A)∣=2k

Proving Set properties

Showing A is Subset of B

To show that AAA is a subset of BBB, we need to show that every element in AAA is also in BBB. The easiest way of doing this is by taking an arbitrary but fixed element from AAA and then showing that it is also in BBB. This would look something like:

Let xxx in A be arbitrary.

x∈A  ⟹  …  ⟹  …  ⟹  x∈B \begin{align*} & x \in A \\ \implies & \dots \\ \implies & \dots \\ \implies & x \in B \end{align*} ⟹⟹⟹​x∈A……x∈B​

Warning

When we say “let x be arbitrary but fixed”, then we mean that we take any element of the set. This means that all of your steps afterwards have to work for any element of the set!

Showing A = B

There are two ways of showing A=BA = BA=B. The first one uses a very useful statement from the script:

A=B⟺A⊆B∧B⊆A A = B \Longleftrightarrow A \subseteq B \land B \subseteq A A=B⟺A⊆B∧B⊆A

This means if we need to show that A=BA = BA=B we can simply show both A⊆BA \subseteq BA⊆B and B⊆AB \subseteq AB⊆A as above.

The second way is by showing directly that any element in AAA is also in BBB and vice versa. A lot of times this also works but might be a little bit more difficult. We let xxx be arbitrary and show:

x∈A⟺…⟺…⟺x∈B \begin{align*} & x \in A \\ \Longleftrightarrow & \dots \\ \Longleftrightarrow & \dots \\ \Longleftrightarrow & x \in B \end{align*} ⟺⟺⟺​x∈A……x∈B​

Note that for this type of proof all your implications need to be double-sided! So you need to make sure that all rows imply the row above and below it!

You can find an example for this in the exercises.

Using Logic

In a lot of cases we can use propositional logic to prove statements regarding sets. Those proofs will mostly follow the same pattern:

  1. Use the definitions to transform a statement or set from set-language into logic-language.
  2. Use propositional logic results to refactor the statement or set
  3. Use the defintions again to get back to set-language

A simple example:

Say we want to work with the set B∪(C∖A)B \cup (C \setminus A)B∪(C∖A). Now:

x∈B∪(C∖A)  ⟹  x∈B∨x∈(C∖A)  ⟹  x∈B∨(x∈C∧¬(x∈A)) \begin{align*} & x \in B \cup (C \setminus A) \\ \implies & x \in B \lor x \in (C \setminus A) \\ \implies & x \in B \lor (x \in C \land \lnot(x \in A)) \end{align*} ⟹⟹​x∈B∪(C∖A)x∈B∨x∈(C∖A)x∈B∨(x∈C∧¬(x∈A))​

Now we can use Lemma 2.1 to refactor the statement and then transform it into a set again with the definitions.

Relations

Look at discmath.ch.

Exercise Sheet Recommendations

Do all the exercises! If you have to leave out some, then skip 4.1 and 4.7, but otherwise try to at least think about all the exercises, because they will give you really good intuition about sets!

item.title: Week6 - Posets, Functions, Countability
item.description:
This week we practice posets and functions and then learn how to prove countability / uncountability.

Resources

  • Exercises + Solutions: pdf
  • Kahoot: link
  • Slides: pdf
  • Exercise Sheet Questions link

There is a great Section about Countability on discmath.ch. You can find more examples there. If cannot quite wrap your head around the concept of different infinities, you can look at this video on youtube.

Notes on Last Exercise Sheet

  • Good work overall
  • Don’t just start with some a and b. Write “Take any a,b …” or “This holds for any a,b in …” or something similar.
  • Jusify your steps!!
  • Don’t make it more complicated than it needs to be. Make sure you exactly understand what you need to show before you start.

Proving Countability of a Set

We know that a set AAA is countable if A≼NA \preccurlyeq \mathbb{N}A≼N, which we can show by finding an injection from AAA to N\mathbb{N}N. But we can also find an injection from AAA to any countable set:

If there is an injection φ:A→B\varphi : A \rightarrow Bφ:A→B and BBB is countable, then AAA is also countable.

Proof: Since BBB is countable we know B≼NB \preccurlyeq \mathbb{N}B≼N and since we found an injection from AAA to BBB we also know A≼BA \preccurlyeq BA≼B. Now the transitivity of ≼\preccurlyeq≼ implies A≼NA \preccurlyeq \mathbb{N}A≼N.

This means we can use some of the countable sets we already know as BBB. Some useful ones are: N\mathbb{N}N, {0,1}∗\{ 0,1 \}^{*}{0,1}∗ (the set of finite bitstrings), N×N\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}N×N or any other countable set that you can create using the rules in the script. So proving countability usually goes like this:

Find the Injection

This is the hardest part. Get an intuition about the set and find the injection φ\varphiφ.

Prove that it is a Function

To prove that φ\varphiφ is a function we need to show that it is well-defined and totally defined. Even if those proprties might seem obvious to you, you still need to prove them!

Prove the Injectivity

Finally, prove that φ\varphiφ is actually an injection.

Conclusion

Conclude with the argument above that the set is countable.

Proving Uncountability

If we want to prove uncountability we first need a lemma:

If BBB is uncountable and there is an injection φ:B→A\varphi : B \rightarrow Aφ:B→A from BBB to AAA then AAA is also uncountable.

Proof: Since there is an injection from BBB to AAA we know that B≼AB \preccurlyeq AB≼A. Now assume AAA was countable. Then A≼NA \preccurlyeq \mathbb{N}A≼N and per injectivity of ≼\preccurlyeq≼ we get B≼NB \preccurlyeq \mathbb{N}B≼N. But this means that BBB is countable, which is a contradiction.

Tip

What you just saw is the magic sentence. Whenever you prove uncountability you will copy-paste this sentence at the start / end of the proof. (Either from your brain or cheatsheet.)

So now we have a method to prove uncountability. Most of the time you will use {0,1}∞\{ 0,1 \}^{\infty}{0,1}∞ as your set BBB.

Find the Injection

This is the hardest part. Get an intuition about the set and find the injection φ\varphiφ.

Prove that it is a Function

To prove that φ\varphiφ is a function we need to show that it is well-defined and totally defined. Even if those proprties might seem obvious to you, you still need to prove them!

Prove the Injectivity

Finally, prove that φ\varphiφ is actually an injection.

Conclusion

Conclude with the magic sentence above that the set is countable.

See that the steps are basically the same as above? Yes! Proving uncountability and countability is not actually that difficult. After you understoof the set you are working with and found the injection, the rest is mostly just mechanical work.

Look at discmath.ch for a more in-depth guide and some useful tips!

Exercise Sheet Recommendations

All the exercises this week are good (and important). Don’t skip 6.6, a lot of (old) exam exercises are similar to it.

item.title: Week9 - Algebra, RSA
item.description:
This week we recap the basics of algebra. Then we take a deep dive into RSA encryption. Lastly, we introduce rings and do some practice exercises.

This week the exercises and everything related to the topic are on the slides.

Notes on Last Exercise Sheet

  • Overall the exercises were very good this week (:
  • You cannot start with what you want to prove! If you do, you arrows have to be reversed (go from bottom to top).

Whenever you define a function (the inverse is a function!), you need to check if it is well-defined. This means that if you base your function definition on a specific representation of an object (for example on aaa) for the equivalence class [a][a][a] then you have to prove that for any representation you choose, you get the same result. I.e. f([a])=f([b])f([a]) = f([b])f([a])=f([b]) should hold if [a]=[b][a] = [b][a]=[b].

Exercise Sheet Recommendations

The three-start exercises are probably not that relevant (for passing the exam), so skip them if you don’t have the time. Otherwise all exercises seem fun. 9.7.1 is very good to practice!

item.title: Week11 - Logic
item.description:
This week we start with chapter 6 - the logic chapter. We talk about proof systems and then cover logical calculi. Lastly we practice some proofs and deriving the conjunctive and disjunctive normal forms.

During the session, we will also answer some of your questions. You can send us quesions through this form: form

Resources

  • Slides + Exercises + Solutions: pdf
  • Kahoot: link
  • Intro Slides: pdf

This week the exercises and everything related to the topic are on the slides.

Notes on Last Exercise Sheet

  • The exercises this week were rather difficult, so don’t be sad if you didn’t get a lot of points
  • Justify your steps! Justify your steps! Justify your steps!
  • Avoid …-notation, it can be dangerous.
  • The neutral elements 0 and 1 of a field have nothing to do with the numbers 0 and 1! They could be any mathematical objects!
  • Be careful about what is being defined in the task. Just because we defined A x B does not mean B x A is also defined.
  • If something is not completely obvious from the definition, then you need to at least write “lemma script” as a justification (if you are using a lemma from the script).
  • Don’t just write “we can now use X to show Y”, show it!

Exercise Sheet Recommendations

Try all of them! Skip the exam exercise if you don’t have time.
